lines.act: ACT ONE — The square that can't be negative
lines.text: Draw the number line, and treat every number as an arrow starting from zero.

lines.act: ACT ONE — The square that can't be negative
lines.text: Now multiply by two. Every arrow gets twice as long. Three lands on six, and minus one lands on minus two.

lines.act: ACT ONE — The square that can't be negative
lines.text: So multiplying by two isn't only a sum. It's a move you apply to the whole line: a stretch.

lines.act: ACT ONE — The square that can't be negative
lines.text: What move is multiplying by minus one?

lines.act: ACT ONE — The square that can't be negative
lines.text: Three goes to minus three. Five goes to minus five. Minus two goes to two.

lines.act: ACT ONE — The square that can't be negative
lines.text: Everything swaps sides. It's a flip through zero.

lines.act: ACT ONE — The square that can't be negative
lines.text: And flip twice, you're back where you started. That's one way to see why a negative times a negative is positive.

lines.act: ACT ONE — The square that can't be negative
lines.text: Now here's the question that causes all the trouble.

lines.act: ACT ONE — The square that can't be negative
lines.text: Is there a number you can multiply by itself to get minus one?

lines.act: ACT ONE — The square that can't be negative
lines.text: In other words, is there a move which, done twice, gives you a flip?

lines.act: ACT ONE — The square that can't be negative
lines.text: Try it on the line. A positive number keeps every arrow on its own side, and doing that twice still keeps it there.

lines.act: ACT ONE — The square that can't be negative
lines.text: A negative number swaps sides, and swapping twice brings you back.

lines.act: ACT ONE — The square that can't be negative
lines.text: Either way, the same move done twice can never end on the opposite side. So on this line, no number squares to minus one.

lines.act: ACT ONE — The square that can't be negative
lines.text: For a long time, that was the end of it. Ask for the square root of a negative, and the honest answer was: that's a badly posed question.

lines.act: ACT ONE — The square that can't be negative
lines.text: And it would have stayed that way, if it hadn't been for an equation that already had a perfectly good answer.

lines.act: ACT TWO — The impossible step to a correct answer
lines.text: In fifteen forty-five, the Italian scholar Gerolamo Cardano published a formula for solving cubic equations, the ones with x cubed in them.

lines.act: ACT TWO — The impossible step to a correct answer
lines.text: But the formula had a strange problem.

lines.act: ACT TWO — The impossible step to a correct answer
lines.text: Take x cubed equals fifteen x plus four.

lines.act: ACT TWO — The impossible step to a correct answer
lines.text: You can check by hand that x equals four works. Four cubed is sixty-four, and fifteen fours plus four is also sixty-four.

lines.act: ACT TWO — The impossible step to a correct answer
lines.text: So there's a real answer, and it's a small whole number.

lines.act: ACT TWO — The impossible step to a correct answer
lines.text: But feed the equation into the formula, and halfway through it asks for the square root of minus one hundred twenty-one.

lines.act: ACT TWO — The impossible step to a correct answer
lines.text: You might think that means the formula simply doesn't apply here. That's what you'd normally conclude when a calculation asks for something impossible.

lines.act: ACT TWO — The impossible step to a correct answer
lines.text: But the answer exists. We just checked it. The formula was pointing at a true result, and its only road went through a number that wasn't allowed.

lines.act: ACT TWO — The impossible step to a correct answer
lines.text: In fifteen seventy-two, an engineer named Rafael Bombelli tried something bold. He ignored the objection and kept calculating.

lines.act: ACT TWO — The impossible step to a correct answer
lines.text: He treated the square root of minus one as an unknown symbol, with one rule: its square is minus one. Otherwise, normal algebra.

lines.act: ACT TWO — The impossible step to a correct answer
lines.text: The formula then wanted two cube roots, and Bombelli found them: two plus that symbol, and two minus that symbol.

lines.act: ACT TWO — The impossible step to a correct answer
lines.text: Now add those. The two and the two make four. The symbols, one plus and one minus, cancel out.

lines.act: ACT TWO — The impossible step to a correct answer
lines.text: Four. The exact right answer, and the impossible part had vanished on the way out.

lines.act: ACT TWO — The impossible step to a correct answer
lines.text: So nobody accepted this number because it sounded nice. It was accepted because it kept producing correct results, while no one could say what it was.

lines.act: ACT TWO — The impossible step to a correct answer
lines.text: In sixteen thirty-seven, Rene Descartes used the word imaginary for quantities like this, and it wasn't meant as a compliment.

lines.act: ACT TWO — The impossible step to a correct answer
lines.text: The symbol we use now, the letter i, came later. But the real question stayed open. A rule isn't an explanation. What is this thing?

lines.act: ACT THREE — A direction nobody had looked in
lines.text: The answer turned up around eighteen hundred, published by Caspar Wessel and then Jean-Robert Argand, working separately.

lines.act: ACT THREE — A direction nobody had looked in
lines.text: And it's almost embarrassingly simple. We already showed no move on the line works. So stop staying on the line.

lines.act: ACT THREE — A direction nobody had looked in
lines.text: Look at that flip again. There's another way to send one to minus one, three to minus three, and everything to its opposite.

lines.act: ACT THREE — A direction nobody had looked in
lines.text: Rotate the whole line half a turn around zero.

lines.act: ACT THREE — A direction nobody had looked in
lines.text: The result looks exactly the same as the flip, but now the move has a middle.

lines.act: ACT THREE — A direction nobody had looked in
lines.text: Stop halfway through the rotation. You've made a quarter turn, and the arrow from zero to one is now pointing straight up, off the line.

lines.act: ACT THREE — A direction nobody had looked in
lines.text: There's your move. A quarter turn, done twice, is a half turn, and a half turn is multiplying by minus one.

lines.act: ACT THREE — A direction nobody had looked in
lines.text: So the square root of minus one isn't a mysterious quantity. It's a quarter turn. And the point one step straight up from zero is what we call i.

lines.act: ACT THREE — A direction nobody had looked in
lines.text: Now we can answer the opening question properly. Walk along the line from one to minus one, and halfway is zero.

lines.act: ACT THREE — A direction nobody had looked in
lines.text: Turn from one to minus one, and halfway is i. Turn the other way around, and halfway is minus i.

lines.act: ACT THREE — A direction nobody had looked in
lines.text: Keep multiplying by i, and you simply keep turning.

lines.act: ACT THREE — A direction nobody had looked in
lines.text: One, then i, then minus one, then minus i, then back to one. Four quarter turns, a full circle.

lines.act: ACT THREE — A direction nobody had looked in
lines.text: So a question that looks terrifying, like i to the power of one hundred, is easy. One hundred is twenty-five full circles, and you end exactly where you began: one.

lines.act: ACT THREE — A direction nobody had looked in
lines.text: The name imaginary makes this sound more mysterious than it is.

lines.act: ACT THREE — A direction nobody had looked in
lines.text: Minus one isn't something you can hold in your hand either. It's a direction on a line. And i is just one more direction, the one we weren't looking in.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The multiplication that turns
lines.text: Once there's a direction up, every point on the page becomes a number.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The multiplication that turns
lines.text: Three to the right and two up is three plus two i. We call these complex numbers, and complex here means built from parts, not difficult.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The multiplication that turns
lines.text: Now test the idea. Multiply three plus two i by i, using plain algebra.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The multiplication that turns
lines.text: Three times i is three i. Two i times i is two i squared, which is minus two.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The multiplication that turns
lines.text: You get minus two plus three i. Now look where that point landed.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The multiplication that turns
lines.text: It's the same arrow, the same length, rotated exactly a quarter turn. Algebra did geometry without being told to.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The multiplication that turns
lines.text: And it works for every complex number, not only i. Each one is an arrow with a length and an angle.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The multiplication that turns
lines.text: When you multiply two of them, the lengths multiply, and the angles add. That's the entire rule.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The multiplication that turns
lines.text: Take one plus i. It points at forty-five degrees, and its length is the square root of two.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The multiplication that turns
lines.text: Square it. The angle doubles to ninety degrees, and the length becomes exactly two. That predicts two i.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The multiplication that turns
lines.text: Check with algebra: one, plus two i, plus i squared. The one and the minus one cancel, and two i is what's left.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The multiplication that turns
lines.text: That rule finally explains the trick from fifteen seventy-two.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The multiplication that turns
lines.text: Bombelli's two plus i is an arrow with an angle of about twenty-six and a half degrees. Cube it, and the angle triples to almost eighty degrees, nearly straight up, landing precisely on two plus eleven i.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The multiplication that turns
lines.text: Its mirror image, two minus i, cubes to two minus eleven i, and that eleven i is the square root of minus one hundred twenty-one.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The multiplication that turns
lines.text: Now add the two arrows. One goes up, its mirror goes down by the same amount, and what's left lies flat on the ordinary line. Two plus two: four.

lines.act: ACT FOUR — The multiplication that turns
lines.text: That's why a real answer had to pass through the imaginary. The formula's path left the line and came back. The real number was the shadow of something happening on the plane.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Why engineers need it
lines.text: So why does the power grid care?

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Why engineers need it
lines.text: The electricity from a wall socket swings forward and back in a smooth wave, around fifty or sixty times every second.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Why engineers need it
lines.text: Picture an arrow turning steadily in a circle, and watch only its height. Up, down, up, down. That height traces out exactly that wave.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Why engineers need it
lines.text: So every smooth wave can be treated as the shadow of a rotating arrow. And we now have numbers that rotate.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Why engineers need it
lines.text: Here's why that helps. Suppose two waves are pushed through the same circuit, one peaking at three volts, the other at four volts, and the second runs a quarter cycle behind the first.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Why engineers need it
lines.text: What's the peak when they combine? You might say seven. It isn't, because they never peak at the same moment.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Why engineers need it
lines.text: With arrows, a quarter cycle is a quarter turn. So the two waves are three and four i, at right angles.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Why engineers need it
lines.text: Add them, and the length is five. The combined wave peaks at exactly five volts.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Why engineers need it
lines.text: Without complex numbers, you could still get that answer, but through pages of trigonometry. With them, it's one short addition.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Why engineers need it
lines.text: Scale that up to a whole circuit, full of coils and capacitors that shift waves in time, and it's the difference between a page of algebra and something truly painful.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Why engineers need it
lines.text: Electrical engineers use this so much that they write the number as j, because i was already taken for current.

lines.act: ACT FIVE — Why engineers need it
lines.text: Radio signals, audio processing, and the equations of quantum mechanics all rely on it as well, for the same basic reason. Things that oscillate are things that turn.

lines.act: ACT SIX — Putting it together
lines.text: Why was anyone forced to accept it? Because a correct answer of four could only be reached by passing through the square root of a negative.

lines.act: ACT SIX — Putting it together
lines.text: What is it? A quarter turn. And the point one step above zero, in a direction the number line never showed us.

lines.act: ACT SIX — Putting it together
lines.text: Why is it useful? Because multiplying complex numbers rotates, and anything that oscillates can be treated as something rotating.

lines.act: ACT SIX — Putting it together
lines.text: So try this with a pencil. Mark any point on a sheet of paper as a number, like two plus i, and multiply it by i four times.

lines.act: ACT SIX — Putting it together
lines.text: Then plot each answer. You won't need anyone to tell you what i means. You'll watch your point walk around a circle and come home.

lines.act: ACT SIX — Putting it together
lines.text: Thanks for watching, and if this made a strange idea feel obvious, subscribe to ninety-nine percent from scratch.
